name: LT3092ETS8#TRPBF
title: 200 mA two-terminal programmable current source
summary: The LT3092 is a current source with only two terminals in use: a precise 10 µA from SET into a resistor sets a voltage that a power amplifier repeats across a second resistor on OUT, so the ratio of the two resistors sets 0.5 mA to 200 mA. It needs 1.2 V to 40 V across it and no input or output capacitors, and it has current limit, thermal shutdown and reverse-voltage and reverse-current protection. TSOT-23-8, SOT-223 and 3 mm × 3 mm DFN-8.

circuits.title: Adjustable 2-terminal current source
circuits.description: The simplest use: RSET from SET and ROUT from OUT meet at the lower terminal. The 10 µA from SET drops 10 µA × RSET across RSET; the amplifier copies that voltage across ROUT, so the current through the two terminals is 10 µA × RSET / ROUT. It works with 1.2 V to 40 V between IN and OUT, with no capacitors.

circuits.title: Series resistors damping long-line reactance
circuits.description: The basic source fed through a long line at each end. A resistor RSERIES in series with the IN lead and another in series with the lower terminal damp the inductance of the lines so the loop stays stable. The resistors cost headroom.

circuits.title: Compensation across the two terminals
circuits.description: A compensation network from IN to the lower terminal. Either a capacitor CCOMP alone (under 1000 pF, or over 1 µF with ESR under 0.5 Ω) or RCOMP in series with CCOMP; the series resistor limits the capacitor's discharge in a fault and lets any capacitor value between those bounds be used.
notes: The alternative is CCOMP alone between IN and the lower terminal, without RCOMP.

circuits.title: Input and output networks to ground
circuits.description: With the source referred to ground, RC networks from IN to ground and from the lower terminal to ground. On the output either COUT alone or ROUT2 in series with COUT; the same value bounds apply as for a capacitor across the source. On the input, 0.1 µF to 1 µF usually does, and it may be larger without limit.
notes: The output network may be COUT alone from the lower terminal to ground.

circuits.title: CSET across RSET for lower noise
circuits.description: The basic source with CSET across RSET to bypass the reference and resistor noise; it also slows start-up by about RSET × CSET. The pole CSET adds usually calls for compensation: RCOMP and CCOMP from IN to the lower terminal.
notes: The compensation may be CCOMP alone, without RCOMP.

circuits.title: Two devices in parallel for 300 mA
circuits.description: Two 150 mA sources share one input and one output. Each has 20 kΩ on SET (200 mV) and 1.33 Ω from OUT to the output; a 300 Ω resistor from the input to each OUT carries part of the current around its device and spreads the heat.

circuits.title: Parallel devices with trace ballast, 400 mA
circuits.description: Two devices with their SET pins tied and one 50 kΩ set resistor (1 V). Each OUT reaches the common node through 40 mΩ of PC trace; R, 2.5 Ω, sets 400 mA. Rx from the input to the common node takes part of the current and the heat.

circuits.title: Paralleling current sources for higher current
circuits.description: Two complete sources side by side with inputs and outputs joined. The total is the sum of the two: IOUT = 10 µA × (R2/R1 + R4/R3).

circuits.title: Paralleling LT3092s with ballast resistor
circuits.description: Two devices with SET pins tied to one 40.2 kΩ resistor. Each OUT has a 40 mΩ ballast to a common node, and 2 Ω from there sets the total of 400 mA.

circuits.title: High voltage current source
circuits.description: Two 100 mA sources stacked in series, each with 20 kΩ (200 mV) and 2 Ω. A 35 V zener across each stage, from its IN to the bottom of its resistors, divides the voltage between the two, so the pair stands off more than one device. IOUT = 200 mV / R1, at least 0.5 mA.

circuits.title: Lower dissipation in a 100 mA source
circuits.description: A 100 mA source (20 kΩ, 2 Ω) with Rx from IN to OUT. Rx carries most of the current so the device dissipates less; Rx = VMAX / (200 mV / R1) × 90%, VMAX being the largest IN-to-OUT voltage.

circuits.title: Capacitor for stability, limited slew rate
circuits.description: A 100 mA source (20 kΩ, 2 Ω) with C1 from IN to OUT. C1 steadies the loop; the voltage across the source can then change no faster than 90% × IOUT / C1.

circuits.title: Remote temperature sensor
circuits.description: A 100 kΩ NTC thermistor (Murata NCP15WF104F03RC, 1%) in parallel with 49.9 kΩ is the set resistance, and 49.9 Ω on OUT sets the current from it. The current runs down the line into a load to ground.

circuits.title: DAC controlled current source
circuits.description: A DAC drives SET directly with 0 V to 1 V, and 10 Ω from OUT to ground makes the current flowing into IN 0.5 mA to 100 mA.

circuits.title: Active load
circuits.description: The device fed from V+, with 10 kΩ on SET and 100 Ω on OUT, both returned to the output node. An NPN sinks 1 mA from the output node to ground, its base driven from the input.

circuits.title: Pulsed current source, load to ground
circuits.description: A 200 mA source (20 kΩ, 1 Ω) feeds a grounded load through a series diode. A VN2222LL from the source's lower node to ground is driven through a gate resistor by an ON/OFF signal.

circuits.title: Fully floating source switching from 200 mA to quiescent
circuits.description: A floating 200 mA source (100 kΩ, 4.99 Ω). The output FET of an NEC PS7801-1A photo-MOS relay sits across the 100 kΩ; when its LED is lit the FET shorts SET to the lower node and the current falls to the device's quiescent current.

circuits.title: Pulsed current source, load to VIN
circuits.description: The load hangs from VIN into IN; a 200 mA source (20 kΩ, 1 Ω) returns to ground through a low-side MOSFET that an OFF/ON signal on its gate turns on and off.

circuits.title: 2-terminal AC current limiter
circuits.description: A diode bridge puts the source (20 kΩ on SET, R = 0.2 V / IOUT on OUT) in the path whichever way the AC current flows, so the two outer terminals limit current in both directions.

circuits.title: Voltage clamp
circuits.description: A current source from VIN to VOUT: 100 kΩ from SET to VOUT, 4.99 Ω from OUT to VOUT. A 10 V zener from VOUT drives the base of a 2N3906 whose emitter sits on a 10 kΩ divider from VIN; its collector drives a 2N3904 that pulls SET to ground. The trip point is VIN − VOUT = 11 V.

circuits.title: High accuracy current source
circuits.description: An LT1634-1.25 shunt reference from SET to the lower node replaces RSET, holding 1.25 V there, and a 124 Ω 0.1% resistor on OUT sets 10 mA.

circuits.title: 2-level current source
circuits.description: A 200 mA source (100 kΩ on SET, 4.99 Ω on OUT) with a foldback that limits the device's dissipation. When VIN − VOUT exceeds about 12 V a 10 V zener raises the gate of a VN2222LL across 10 kΩ; the FET puts a second 100 kΩ in parallel with the first and the current drops to 100 mA.
notes: IOUT is 200 mA while VIN − VOUT is under 12 V and 100 mA above it.

circuits.title: More efficient current source
circuits.description: An LT3470A buck converter from 36 V supplies IN of a 200 mA source (20 kΩ, 1 Ω). A ZVP3306F, with its gate on the source's lower node and 100 Ω from the converter output, feeds the converter's FB so its output tracks a little above the voltage the source needs, keeping the device's dissipation low.

circuits.title: USB LED driver
circuits.description: From a USB supply, a 200 mA source (20 kΩ, 1 Ω) drives an LED to ground.

circuits.title: Current limiter for remote power
circuits.description: The source in series with a long supply line to a remote LDO: a 100 kΩ potentiometer on SET adjusts the limit, 4.99 Ω on OUT. The LDO at the far end has capacitors on its input and output.

operation.text: A 10 µA reference with a near-zero temperature coefficient flows out of SET into the non-inverting input of a power amplifier, whose output buffers that voltage at OUT. All bias current returns through OUT, so the part is a two-terminal source between IN and the far ends of its two resistors. It runs with or without capacitors at its terminals.

Pick RSET first so the SET voltage swamps the SET-to-OUT offset: around 200 mV (20 kΩ) leaves errors of a few percent from offset; smaller voltages raise that error, larger ones cost headroom. ROUT then follows from the ratio, and its tolerance adds to the error. The current depends on the ratio of the two, so resistors of the same material that track each other give a low tempco without low-ppm parts.
The part does not regulate below 0.5 mA; its own quiescent current (300 µA typical, 500 µA maximum) flows to OUT.

Many applications need no capacitor at all, given a tight, low-reactance layout. Long leads or traces add inductance that can cause oscillation; resistance in series with the input and output lines can damp it, and at currents under about 5 mA the large programming resistors often damp it alone. Otherwise a capacitor across the source works if it is under 1000 pF or over 1 µF with ESR under 0.5 Ω; a series RC (typically 100 Ω to about 5 kΩ) allows values in between and limits the discharge current in a fault. A capacitor across RSET adds a pole that usually needs such compensation. Stability is to be confirmed in the final circuit under all conditions.

A ground-referred source may need its top bypassed to ground, with the same bounds (under 1000 pF, or over 1 µF with ESR under 0.5 Ω, or a series RC); an existing supply output capacitor may already do it. On the high-impedance input those bounds do not apply: 0.1 µF to 1 µF is usually enough and more does no harm. Long supply wires and a low-ESR input capacitor can ring as a high-Q tank; 0.1 Ω to 1 Ω in series with the input or the capacitor damps it. In the hardest cases networks on both input and output may be needed.

Z5U and Y5V dielectrics lose much of their value with DC bias and temperature: a 16 V 10 µF Y5V part can fall to 1 µF to 2 µF at 5 V across temperature. X5R and X7R hold value better (X7R over temperature; X5R is cheaper and comes larger), but bias loss can still be large, less so in larger cases. Some ceramics are piezoelectric and turn vibration or thermal shock into voltage.

The 10 µA reference has about 2.7 pA/√Hz of noise, 0.7 nA RMS from 10 Hz to 100 kHz. The set resistor adds its thermal noise. CSET across RSET bypasses both; it lengthens start-up in proportion to RSET × CSET and gives a soft start, and usually needs compensation.

10 nA of leakage into or out of SET and its network is a 0.1% error in the reference current. Use good insulation (Teflon, Kel-F), clean off flux, consider a conformal coat in humid conditions, and surround SET with a guard ring on both sides of the board driven from OUT; bulk leakage falls as the ring gets wider.

Two or more complete sources can share input and output and add their currents. Alternatively, tie the SET pins and the IN pins and join the outputs through short PC traces as ballast. With an offset of at most ±2 mV at room temperature, 40 mΩ per device gives better than 80% current sharing at full output, and the 20 mΩ of two in parallel costs about 8 mV of compliance at 0.4 A. Spreading the devices spreads the heat; input resistors can carry some of the power at high input voltage.

Keep the junction at or below 125°C in continuous use, counting every thermal path from junction to air and any nearby heat sources. Surface-mount packages sink heat into board copper, planes and vias. The DFN exposed pad and the SOT-223 tab are at VOUT. Demo board 1531A, with several inner VOUT planes and thermal vias, reaches 28°C/W for the DFN.

Current limiting and thermal shutdown (typically 165°C, about 5°C hysteresis) guard against overload. IN withstands ±40 V relative to SET and OUT, so reversed input and output are survived. If OUT rises above IN, reverse current is under 1 mA, typically under 100 µA. SET is clamped to OUT by diodes with 1 kΩ resistors, rated for ±10 V and ±15 mA between the pins; they conduct only in transients.

E and I grades cover –40°C to 125°C junction and MP covers –55°C to 125°C; I and MP are guaranteed across their full range, E is tested at 25°C with the extremes assured by design and characterization.
